Amon
AY-muhn
proper noun (figure)
Hebrew Amon (H526) — possibly "skilled workman" (from aman, "to nurture, support, be faithful") or "hidden" (cognate with the Egyptian god Amun, whom his idolatrous father Manasseh may have honored in naming him). The Hebrew root produces both amen ("truly, faithful") and omanut ("craftsmanship"); the ambiguity of the king's name is itself a small commentary on his confused inheritance.

📖 Biblical Definition

Amon (c. 642 — 640 BC) was the fifteenth king of Judah (2 Kings 21:19-26; 2 Chronicles 33:21-25), son of the deeply apostate Manasseh, father of the great reformer Josiah, whose two-year reign was so brief and so wicked that the canonical record dispatches him in less than half a chapter in each account. Twenty-two years old at his accession; reigned two years; assassinated by his own servants in his palace at age twenty-four. The Chronicler's verdict is unsparing: "he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, as did Manasseh his father: for Amon sacrificed unto all the carved images which Manasseh his father had made, and served them; And humbled not himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself; but Amon trespassed more and more" (2 Chr 33:22-23). The phrase "trespassed more and more" sets him below his father: Manasseh had at least repented at the end of his long reign in Assyrian captivity (2 Chr 33:12-13), but Amon refused that humbling and continued the idolatry without the late-life remorse. His assassination is recorded without dynastic crisis: the people of Judah killed his assassins and made his eight-year-old son Josiah king in his place, an extraordinary popular intervention that preserved the Davidic line through the boy who would become the greatest reform-king of the divided monarchy. The Chronicler's silence on Amon's burial (he was buried in the garden of Uzza, his father's burial place, 2 Kings 21:26, rather than in the royal tombs) is itself a final commentary. The two-year reign is one of the shortest in the canonical record; the assassination one of the few palace coups in Davidic-Judah history; the popular intervention to install Josiah one of the most extraordinary moments of divine providence preserving the Davidic line.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Fifteenth king of Judah (c. 642-640 BC); son of Manasseh; father of Josiah; reigned only 2 years; assassinated by his own servants; the Chronicler's verdict: 'trespassed more and more' (refused the late-life humbling that even his father Manasseh had received).

AMON, proper noun. Hebrew Amon (H526) — possibly "skilled workman" (from aman) or echoing the Egyptian god name. Distinct from Ammon (a different Hebrew name and the related people group).

Fifteenth king of Judah (c. 642-640 BC); son of Manasseh; father of Josiah.

Reigned only 2 years; assassinated by his own servants in the palace; the people then killed the assassins and made his eight-year-old son Josiah king.

Verdict: 'did evil in the sight of the LORD as did Manasseh his father... humbled not himself... trespassed more and more' (2 Chr 33:22-23).

📖 Key Scripture

2 Chronicles 33:22-23 — "But [Amon] did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, as did Manasseh his father: for Amon sacrificed unto all the carved images which Manasseh his father had made, and served them; And humbled not himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself; but Amon trespassed more and more."

2 Kings 21:23-24 — "And the servants of Amon conspired against him, and slew the king in his own house. And the people of the land slew all them that had conspired against king Amon; and the people of the land made Josiah his son king in his stead."

Zephaniah 1:1 — "The word of the LORD which came unto Zephaniah... in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah."

Matthew 1:10 — "And Ezekias begat Manasses; and Manasses begat Amon; and Amon begat Josias."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Amon is corrupted when his short wicked reign is treated as merely an interlude between Manasseh's drama and Josiah's reform rather than as a serious doctrinal warning about generational reception of repentance, when his refusal of his father's late-life humbling is overlooked, or when the popular intervention to install Josiah is treated as political accident rather than divine providence.

expand to see more

Interlude misreading. Amon's two-year reign and assassination are often skipped in popular Bible reading: a wicked father (Manasseh), a wicked son (Amon), and then the great reformer Josiah. The Chronicler's careful theological framing resists this skip. Amon was offered the same Yahweh that his father had finally come to in Assyrian captivity; Amon refused. The verdict 'humbled not himself, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself; but Amon trespassed more and more' (2 Chr 33:23) means the son had access to his father's late-life testimony and turned away from it. The doctrinal lesson is generational and severe: each generation must receive the gospel personally; no son is automatically saved by his father's eventual repentance.

Popular-intervention as accident. The episode in 2 Kings 21:24 and 2 Chr 33:25 — the people of the land killing Amon's assassins and installing his eight-year-old son Josiah — is not a colorful political vignette. The Chronicler is making a theological point: the LORD preserved the Davidic line through popular intervention against a coup that could easily have ended the dynasty. Eight-year-old Josiah survived because Judah's covenant-people refused to accept a non-Davidic king. The text is celebrating the LORD's faithfulness to 2 Samuel 7:16 through the agency of the people of the land.
